subject: religious-studies
title: Branches of Christianity
welcome_lead: From Constantinople to Wittenberg to Lambeth — explore the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions.
meta_desc: Religious Studies Adventure: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christianity.
final_note: You have walked through Christianity's main branches. Diversity within unity remains a defining feature.

concepts.def: Largest Christian communion, led by the Pope (Bishop of Rome), with around 1.4 billion members.
Communion of autocephalous churches united by liturgy and the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Family of non-Chalcedonian churches including Coptic and Armenian Orthodox.
Western Christian movement originating in the Reformation, emphasising sola scriptura and sola fide.
Tradition tracing to the English Reformation, balancing Catholic and Reformed elements.
Fastest-growing Protestant movement emphasising Holy Spirit gifts, originating in early 20th century revivals.

walkthroughs.body_html: The 1054 mutual excommunications between Rome and Constantinople formalised divisions over papal authority, filioque, leavened/unleavened bread and other issues. Eastern Orthodoxy emphasises consensus among autocephalous churches and the deifying transformation (theosis) of believers.

Martin Luther's 95 Theses (1517) launched the Reformation. Calvin in Geneva, Zwingli in Zurich, the radical Anabaptists and Henry VIII's English Reformation produced diverse traditions. The Council of Trent (1545-63) shaped Catholic responses.

Pope Francis (since 2013) leads the Catholic Church. Vatican II (1962-65) reformed liturgy and ecumenical relations. Pentecostalism has expanded rapidly in Latin America, Africa and Asia. The global Christian population is estimated at around 2.4 billion.

mcqs.q: How did Hume define a miracle?
options: Hume defined a miracle as something amazing or unexpected.
Hume believed all miracles in the Bible really happened.
The Quran was written by Allah and dropped from heaven.
A violation of the laws of nature by a particular volition of the Deity — and he argued evidence for such violations could never outweigh the uniform experience supporting the laws.
